title: What is a case interview, and what are interviewers really looking for?
description: What a case interview is, the two formats you will meet, and the six things every interviewer scores.
hook: A case interview is a 20 to 40 minute conversation in which you solve a business problem out loud, and interviewers are looking less for the right answer than for how you get there. They want to see you break the problem into parts, test ideas with numbers, and land on a clear recommendation, while sounding like someone they could put in front of a client. This guide explains the two formats you will meet and the six things almost every interviewer scores.

In this guide

  • What a case interview is
  • The two questions behind every score
  • Interviewer-led and candidate-led cases
  • The six things interviewers score
  • A worked example: the bakery chain
  • What strong and weak sound like
  • Four myths that waste your preparation
  • Check yourself
  • Where to go next

What a case interview is

A case interview is a business problem handed to you in a sentence or two: profits are falling, should we enter this market, what should we charge. It usually takes 20 to 40 minutes of a longer interview that also includes questions about you. Nobody expects you to know the answer. The interviewer wants to watch you do, in miniature, what a consultant does on a project: work out what the client actually needs, break the problem into parts, find the part that matters, use data to test your ideas and finish with a recommendation the client could act on.

The firms say this themselves. McKinsey describes its problem-solving interview as a conversation with no single logical solution, and Bain's case interview page says it is not looking for one right answer. So stop treating the case as a quiz with a hidden password. It is a test of how you think, in public.

The two questions behind every score

However the scorecard is laid out, the interviewer is answering two questions about you:

  1. Can this person solve the problem? Is the structure sensible, are the numbers right, does the conclusion follow from the evidence?
  2. Would I put this person in front of a client? Are they clear, calm and easy to follow? Do they listen, take a hint and recover from a mistake?

The second question is judged on every sentence you say, not just at the end. Plenty of candidates reach the right number and still fail because the route there was hard to follow. That is why the PrepForCase course gives a whole lesson to how you come across.

Interviewer-led and candidate-led cases

You will meet two styles, and the difference is who holds the steering wheel.

Interviewer-led

The interviewer moves you through the case question by question: first a structure, then a calculation, then a chart, then a recommendation. Each answer is judged largely on its own. McKinsey is widely known for this style, though it varies by office and interviewer. The trap is passivity: even here, you earn credit for linking each answer back to the goal and saying what you would look at next.

Candidate-led

You get the prompt and are expected to drive. You decide which part of your structure to test first, ask for the data you need and say when you have enough to move on. BCG and Bain cases are usually run this way, as are those at most other firms. The most common way to lose a candidate-led case is to wait to be told what to do. See how to drive a case for the habits that fix this.

Prepare for both. The skills are the same; only the amount of steering changes. A candidate who can drive will do well in an interviewer-led case too.

The six things interviewers score

Firms' scorecards differ in wording, but most cover these six skills. The PrepForCase case log scores your practice on the same six, so you can see which one is holding you back.

SkillWhat the interviewer watches for
Clarify and recapYou restate the problem in your own words, confirm the goal and ask two or three questions that matter.
Structure and hypothesisA MECE breakdown tailored to this client, and a view on where to start.
Maths and chartsCorrect numbers, worked out loud, with the so-what stated after every result.
Case leadershipYou propose the next step after every answer rather than waiting.
RecommendationAnswer first, two or three reasons with numbers, risks and next steps, in about 60 seconds.
CommunicationShort sentences, signposting, a calm voice and no rambling.

Notice that only one of the six is about maths. Many candidates spend most of their preparation on frameworks and arithmetic and almost none on the opening, the close or their delivery. Practise all six.

A worked example: the bakery chain

Here is how the first ten minutes of a typical case unfold. The figures are illustrative.

Interviewer: "Our client is a regional bakery chain. Sales are flat at about $4M a year, but profit has fallen by a third. The CEO wants to know why and what to do."

Recap and clarify. A strong candidate replays the problem in one breath and checks the goal: "So: a regional bakery chain, revenue flat at $4M, profit down a third, and we need the cause and a fix. Is the goal to get back to last year's profit, and by when? And is the whole bakery market seeing this, or just our client?" The interviewer says the goal is to recover within a year, and competitors are doing fine. That one answer points the case inside the company.

Structure. Profit = revenue − costs. Revenue is flat, so the candidate says the hypothesis is that costs have risen, and proposes to split costs into ingredients, labour, rent and other.

Maths. The interviewer shares the numbers:

LineLast yearThis yearChange
Revenue$4.00M$4.00M$0
Ingredients$1.40M$1.55M+$150k
Labour$1.20M$1.24M+$40k
Rent$0.60M$0.60M$0
Other$0.20M$0.21M+$10k
Profit$600k$400k−$200k

Total costs rose from $3.4M to $3.6M, so profit fell from $600k to $400k: $200k, or one third. Ingredients account for $150k of the $200k, which is 75% of the drop, and ingredient spend itself rose about 11% ($150k ÷ $1.4M).

The so-what. "Ingredients explain three quarters of the fall, so that is where I would go next. I'd like to know whether it is the price we pay for flour and butter, or whether we are using or wasting more." That sentence is the moment the interviewer starts to trust you: a number, what it means for the goal, and a next step.

What strong and weak sound like

Take the same moment, straight after the cost table appears.

Weak: "OK, so ingredients went up, labour went up a bit, rent stayed the same and other costs went up slightly."
Strong: "Ingredients are 75% of the $200k drop. Labour is only $40k. So I'd park labour and dig into ingredients: price per kilo first, then usage and waste."

The weak answer describes the table. The strong one ranks the drivers, puts a number on the biggest, and moves the case on. You can practise this exact habit every day: after any analysis, finish the sentence "This tells us __, which matters because the client wants __, so next I would look at __."

Four myths that waste your preparation

  • "I need to know the industry." You need to ask good questions about it. Interviewers give you the facts that matter. Basic knowledge of how businesses make money is enough to start.
  • "There is a framework for every case." Frameworks are starting shapes, not answers. McKinsey explicitly asks candidates to tailor their approach rather than apply a standard framework. Learn the common ones in which framework to use, then adapt them.
  • "The maths is the hard part." The arithmetic rarely goes beyond percentages, multiplication and division. Doing it out loud, under pressure, without dropping a zero is the skill.
  • "If I get the answer, I pass." Two candidates can reach the same answer. The one who defined the problem, isolated the driver and explained the action is the one who gets the offer.

Check yourself

Have a go at each before you open the answer.

1. In a candidate-led case, what is the most common way to lose points?

Show the answer

Waiting for the interviewer to say what to do next. Candidate-led cases reward you for driving. After every answer, say where you want to go next and why.

2. Which clarifying question best splits a profitability case in two?

Show the answer

"Is the whole industry affected, or just our client?" An industry-wide problem points to market causes such as input prices or demand. A company-only problem points to the client's own revenue or costs.

3. A cinema chain's ticket sales have fallen 15% in two years. What is your one clarifying question, and why?

Show the answer

"Is the whole cinema industry seeing this decline, or just our client?" If it is industry-wide, look at streaming, release schedules and viewing habits. If it is only our client, look at locations, prices, film choice and the experience in the cinema.

4. In the bakery example, revenue had instead fallen from $4M to $3.8M while costs stayed at $3.4M. What changes?

Show the answer

Profit would be $3.8M − $3.4M = $400k, the same one-third fall, but the cause is now entirely revenue. You would split revenue into number of transactions × average spend, and by store or product, to find where the $200k went.
